title: Disaster-resilience funding becomes a lived public-system outcome only when grant review, policy continuity, and measurement work
source_unit: U.S. Government Accountability Office, FEMA: Billions in Building Resilient Infrastructure and Communities Subgrants Remain Unawarded (GAO-26-107774)
geography: United States; FEMA BRIC applicants and subapplicants across states, territories, Tribes, and local governments

observations.period: Fiscal years 2020-2023 grant cycles; status as of March 2025

denominator.unit: BRIC subapplications analyzed across four grant cycles

allocated_funding.unit: billion dollars allocated against 4.8 billion dollars available

completed_closeout.unit: subgrants with completed work and initiated closeout

mechanism.value: A grant award is not equivalent to implemented resilience; obligation, reimbursement, construction, and closeout are separate conversion points

observations.method: GAO analysis of FEMA BRIC documentation and program data from four grant cycles, supplemented by interviews with selected states, communities, and FEMA officials.
observations.uncertainty: The figures describe BRIC administrative status rather than the full universe of resilience investment or verified hazard-loss reduction; reimbursement and closeout can lag physical work.
observations.subgroup: Local governments, states, Tribes, territories, and economically disadvantaged rural communities applying for hazard-mitigation support.
observations.counterinterpretation: A low completed-closeout count may partly reflect the long duration of infrastructure projects and administrative timing rather than project failure.

denominator.unit: BRIC subapplications awaiting FEMA award decisions after the second review stage had not been completed

associated_funding.unit: billion dollars associated with pending subapplications

median_review_time.value: 7 to 9 months to finalize review and award

local_cost_pressure.value: Communities reported that review delays could extend project timelines and increase costs

mechanism.value: Administrative time is an infrastructure cost: delay can erode purchasing power, contractor availability, and local planning certainty

observations.method: GAO analysis of FEMA review-stage data and interviews with selected state and community officials.
observations.uncertainty: Reported cost effects were not estimated as a national causal total; interviewed communities were a nongeneralizable selection.
observations.subgroup: Applicants with limited staff, changing construction prices, hazard exposure, or little ability to absorb schedule slippage.
observations.counterinterpretation: Review safeguards may prevent poorly designed or non-cost-effective projects, so faster processing is not automatically better processing.

denominator.unit: federal grant-program transition reviewed by GAO

policy_sequence.value: FEMA announced BRIC termination in April 2025 and restart in March 2026

communication_gap.value: FEMA did not clarify which subgrants would be terminated during the intervening period

work_stoppage.value: State officials reported that some subrecipients stopped work because of funding uncertainty

mechanism.value: Policy volatility and unclear communication can freeze local action even when money and project demand exist

observations.method: GAO review of FEMA advisories and interviews with selected state and community officials.
observations.uncertainty: The report does not quantify how many projects stopped or isolate communication from other causes of delay.
observations.subgroup: State agencies, local governments, Tribes, contractors, and residents awaiting mitigation investments.
observations.counterinterpretation: Program changes may reflect legitimate reprioritization or legal and fiscal constraints; clearer communication would not by itself resolve funding scarcity.

observations.period: Fiscal year 2023 and fiscal years 2024-2025 BRIC program design

denominator.unit: BRIC funding-cycle designs compared by GAO

performance_boundary.value: FEMA established goals but did not consistently define methods and targets to measure results or use performance information in the termination decision

design_shift.value: The newer cycle emphasized construction-ready infrastructure, faster obligation, and greater state, territory, and Tribal responsibility

planning_change.value: Direct technical assistance and some stand-alone planning activities were removed or narrowed in the newer cycle

mechanism.value: A speed-and-construction focus can improve delivery while weakening upstream planning and capacity support for places least able to prepare projects

observations.method: GAO comparison of FEMA BRIC notices of funding opportunity, performance goals, administrative data, and program-management practices.
observations.uncertainty: The report does not yet show whether the revised cycle will shorten reviews, improve geographic equity, or reduce future disaster losses.
observations.subgroup: Smaller, rural, Tribal, disadvantaged, and technically constrained communities facing high hazard exposure.
observations.counterinterpretation: Prioritizing construction-ready projects and shifting responsibility to states or Tribes could reduce federal bottlenecks and speed implementation if those governments have sufficient capacity.

FEMA BRIC program page for program context.

boundary: This record captures a public-system conversion problem: resilience need and federal appropriations pass through review time, policy continuity, communication, local capacity, and outcome measurement before they become completed protective infrastructure. It is a GAO administrative and interview-based audit, not a national estimate of avoided disaster losses or a respondent-level household study.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: The official GAO report page and full HTML report were reviewed for BRIC awards, pending review, reimbursement, program transition, performance-management, and funding-cycle design findings.
